voiceover.text: Last time, the WHO definition gave health three dimensions: physical, mental and social. It's tempting to treat them as three separate scores. But think about a student who tears a hamstring. A scan would find one physical injury. Yet within two months, their friendships, their mood and even their recovery have all changed. So why doesn't an injury stay in the dimension it started in?

Follow it step by step. The torn hamstring means they can't train, so they stop seeing their team three times a week. That's a social change. Two months without the team, and without the thing they're good at, and their mood drops. That's a mental change. A low mood makes the rehab exercises harder to keep doing, so the physical recovery slows down. The change has travelled from physical, to social, to mental, and back to physical. It's a loop.

That's what the syllabus means by dimensions interacting. A change in one dimension causes a change in another, and it can run back to where it started. So an answer that lists the dimensions one by one hasn't explained anything yet. Put a mechanism on every arrow. And the loop can run the good way too. Joining a social sports team lifts the social dimension, which supports mood, which makes it more likely the person keeps exercising. One change, three dimensions.

So what counts as good health? It isn't one bar that everyone is measured against. A seventeen-year-old sprinter who's back to jogging after an illness would call their health poor. A seventy-year-old who walks two kilometres a day, and takes medication for blood pressure, would call a similar level of fitness excellent. Both are right, because good health is judged relative to a person's circumstances, expectations and life stage. That's why someone can live with a chronic condition and still be in good health.

To describe health that keeps moving, we use the health continuum. It's a line, not a switch, with optimal health at one end and death at the other. Everyone is somewhere on it, and nobody stays still. Now put two people at exactly the same point. One is three weeks into recovering from an injury, moving towards optimal health. The other has an untreated condition that's slowly getting worse. Their position is identical, but their situations are opposite.

So a position on its own doesn't describe anyone's health. You also need direction, which way they're moving, and rate, how fast. A broken wrist moves you sharply and briefly. A slowly developing condition moves you so gradually that nobody notices. The model has one big limitation, though. A single line can't show the dimensions moving in different directions at once, like a body that's recovering while mood is falling.

Health also changes on different timescales, and each one has different causes. Within a day or a week, it's sleep, food, stress or a passing cold, fast and mostly reversible. Across months and years, it's habits building up, a condition developing, or a job changing, slow enough to be invisible while it happens. And across a whole life, life stage changes what health even means. The slow timescale matters most, and it's the one noticed least.

The last part of the dot point is about circumstances, the conditions of a person's life, like income, housing, work, relationships, location and access to services. Most of them aren't choices. Circumstances change health in two ways. The first is direct. Imagine a family whose income falls when a parent loses their job. They move to cheaper, more crowded housing, sleep gets broken, and the food gets cheaper. Health changes without anyone deciding anything about health.

The second way is quieter. Circumstances change the range of choices a person actually has. The teenager in that family starts working shifts after school, so training stops. Exercise hasn't become less important to them. It's become less available. And because circumstances keep changing, a new job or a scholarship could move their health back the other way. So health is dynamic, which means always changing, for reasons you can name: the dimensions interact, people move along the continuum, and the conditions around them keep shifting.
Two lines to remember. Position isn't the whole story, so describe direction and rate. And circumstances change health directly, and they change which choices are possible.
Two exam questions. First. Two people are placed at the same point on the health continuum. Explain why this information alone does not describe their health. Pause here to answer.

A position is only a snapshot. One person could be recovering and moving towards optimal health, while the other is getting worse, so you need their direction and rate as well. And one line can't show their dimensions moving differently. The classic mistake is saying they must have the same health because they're at the same point.
Second. Explain the dynamic nature of health, referring to the dimensions of health and the health continuum. Pause here to answer.

Define dynamic first: health changes, for reasons you can name. Then give two mechanisms. The dimensions interact, so an injury can lower social contact, then mood, then slow recovery. And the continuum shows that people at one position can move in opposite directions, so you describe direction and rate. The classic mistake is defining both terms and never using them.

So, to explain why someone's health is changing, name the interaction, the direction and rate, and the circumstance behind it. So far that's one person at a time. Next, we'll zoom out to a whole population, and ask how you can measure the health of millions of people at once.
